Bodies as Living Archives

Remembering Korean War POWs in Taiwan

A digital exhibition by Hsiao-Chi Chu, exploring how official Cold War narratives meet the testimonies, gestures, bodies and later lives of former prisoners of war.

Hsiao-Chi Chu1950–2018TaiwanEnglish / 繁體中文
Explore the exhibition ↘Open original Tumblr ↗
01   /   The story

Between a state narrative and a lived history

In 1954, more than 14,000 Chinese prisoners of war from the Korean War came to Taiwan and were publicly represented as “Anti-Communist Heroes” within Taiwan’s Cold War political narrative. Decades later, their experiences of war, displacement, political ideology and resettlement remain not only in official archives, but also in personal testimonies, gestures, silences and ageing bodies. Drawing on my socially engaged art practice with former POWs at the Taipei Veterans Home between 2014 and 2018, this story explores the body as a living archive through which established public narratives can be revisited and complicated. It asks who has the authority to decide how these men should be remembered: the state, the archive, or those whose bodies and memories carry this history themselves?

閱讀中文版 · Read the original Chinese description

1954年，一萬四千多名中國籍韓戰戰俘來到台灣，並在台灣的冷戰政治敘事中被塑造成「反共義士」。數十年後，他們對戰爭、流離失所、政治意識形態與重新安置的經驗，不只存在於官方檔案，也留存在個人的證言、動作、沉默與逐漸老去的身體之中。透過我2014年至2018年間與台北榮民之家前韓戰戰俘共同進行的社會參與式藝術實踐，這個故事將「身體」視為一座活的檔案，藉此重新觀看並複雜化既有的公共歷史敘事。它進一步追問：究竟誰有權決定這些人應該如何被記憶？是國家、檔案，還是那些以自己的身體與記憶承載這段歷史的人？

Who has the authority to decide how Korean War POWs in Taiwan should be remembered: the state, the archive, or the people whose bodies and memories carry this history?
Curatorial note · Reading historical language

The label “Anti-Communist Heroes” (反共義士) is reproduced as part of Taiwan’s Cold War political vocabulary, not as a neutral description of the men. The exhibition also addresses war captivity, political coercion, tattoos and bodily evidence. Such sources must be interpreted with attention to provenance, consent, context and the limits of what another person’s body can tell us.

03   /   Reading the archives

The political life of memory

The story begins with the Korean War and the arrival of more than 14,000 Chinese POWs in Taiwan in 1954. The public language attached to their arrival—freedom, loyalty, anti-communism and return—became part of a highly visible political programme. Official celebrations, memorial objects and institutional records helped shape a collective image of these men.

The original exhibition examines objects and places at the Taipei Veterans Home, including the Freedom Bell, the Statue of Freedom and the commemorative landscape of Zhongyi Villa (忠義山莊). The inscriptions and monuments are important evidence of what institutions wanted to memorialise. They do not, by themselves, resolve the diversity of individual wartime experiences.

Words used on monuments and in official records are therefore presented as historical evidence in their own right. Reading them critically requires asking who produced an inscription, what public it addressed, and how a political narrative changed—or concealed—the experiences it claimed to describe.

04   /   Embodied evidence

What a body remembers

Beyond the official archive, the exhibition attends to testimony, bodily marks, habits and silence. Tattoos, gestures and the material traces of later life may disclose personal histories that an institutional record cannot fully contain. Yet none of these signs has a single, self-evident meaning: conviction, coercion, adaptation and survival may be entangled.

In the work’s account, the distinction between an official archive and a “living archive” is methodological. Archives preserve documents and institutional labels. Embodied memory emerges through lived experience and through encounters between people. Both require careful interpretation; neither should be treated as transparent access to the past.

05   /   Artistic research

Art as a form of encounter

Between 2014 and 2018, Chu’s socially engaged art practice with former prisoners of war at the Taipei Veterans Home approached participants as collaborators. The project’s source base includes field notes, testimonies, photographs and artworks produced in conversation with the men and their communities.

Bodily Folds: Hidden / Inducing the Body · 2014

This cross-generational project brought together Bu-Ting Zhang, Hsiao-Chi Chu and Yong-Chi Ku. It explored bodily perception, experience and knowledge while asking how relationships shape the people taking part in an artistic encounter. The creator’s reflections also acknowledge practical and ethical constraints, including health, trust, repeated visits and the need to know when to step back.

Zhongyi Eatery (Zhongyi Snack Bar) · 2018

In a later collaborative project, Shi-Gao Guo, Hsiao-Chi Chu and Shiu-Yuan Yu used food, calligraphy and shared making to approach memory through practice. Rather than appearing only as subjects of a history told by others, the veterans contributed skills and creative knowledge of their own.

Curatorial note · Testimony and participation

Material involving living or recently deceased participants demands particular care. A photograph or gesture may be documentary evidence without making the person’s private experience freely available. The original Tumblr posts remain the primary location for the creator’s visual documentation, contextual explanations and attribution.

Why the story matters

The “Anti-Communist Heroes” were once highly visible political symbols in Cold War Taiwan, yet the complexity of their individual experiences has become far less visible. Revisiting their lives through testimony, artistic practice and embodied memory invites audiences to consider how states, archives and individuals produce different versions of the past. Beyond Taiwan, the story contributes to wider conversations about Cold War history, displacement and the politics of memory in East Asia. It ultimately raises a question relevant to public history across different contexts: who has the authority to determine how difficult histories are remembered?

1950–1953

The Korean War and the experiences of Chinese prisoners of war form the historical background.

1954

More than 14,000 Chinese POWs arrive in Taiwan, where Cold War public commemorations cast them as “Anti-Communist Heroes.”

1970s

Monuments and commemorative objects at Zhongyi Villa and the veterans home continue to shape institutional remembrance.

2014

Bodily Folds: cross-generational artistic work begins to explore embodied memory through collaboration.

2018

Zhongyi Eatery: food, skill and shared creation offer further ways of engaging with lived history.
